* **Al cierre del cuarto año de la administración, las finanzas públicas continúan con un manejo responsable de los recursos públicos, un nivel estable de la deuda y un ejercicio eficiente del gasto orientado al bienestar de las familias mexicanas.**
* **La deuda pública se ubicó en 49.4% del PIB, un nivel menor respecto a lo presupuestado para 2022 y al observado en 2021, en 1.6 y 1.4 puntos porcentuales del PIB, respectivamente. Este resultado fue posible por el buen desempeño de los ingresos presupuestarios, que aún después del subsidio al IEPS, fueron mayores a lo presupuestado en 1.5% del PIB.**
* **La economía mexicana mostró en 2022 un mejor desempeño que el esperado por los analistas al acumular un crecimiento de 2.9% a noviembre, apoyado por el buen desempeño del mercado laboral, el consumo y la inversión privada.**
* **Al cierre de 2022, se registraron las tasas de desempleo más bajas en 17 años: 2.8% en el total y 2.5% para las mujeres, debido a la creación de 2.4 millones de plazas de trabajo en 2022, en su mayoría formales. La mejora en las condiciones laborales contribuyó a que el consumo privado acumulara hasta octubre de 2022 un crecimiento de 7.1%, tasa superior en más del doble a su promedio histórico.**
* **La confianza en la economía mexicana por parte de los inversionistas extranjeros logró que, al 3er trimestre de 2022, el flujo de inversión extranjera directa (IED) fuera de 32 mil millones de dólares, nivel no visto desde 2013.**

*Resumen ejecutivo*

* Al cierre de 2022, las disrupciones en las cadenas de suministro y los costos de transporte disminuyeron, lo cual aminoró las presiones inflacionarias.
* Se observaron sorpresas positivas en indicadores oportunos y adelantados de las principales economías del mundo, las cuales han llevado a los analistas a mejorar sus estimaciones de crecimiento económico global para 2022.
* Para 2023, el crecimiento de la actividad a nivel mundial podría ser mayor al esperado (actualmente de 2.1% anual), ya que estará apoyado de la reapertura económica de China y los menores precios de materias primas.
* Con respecto a la economía mexicana, el consumo privado acumuló un crecimiento de 7.1% a octubre de 2022, superior a su promedio histórico de 2.7%. En su interior, el consumo de servicios ya recuperó sus niveles previos a la pandemia.
* La inversión fija bruta acumuló un crecimiento anual de 5.5% a octubre, superior al promedio histórico para un mismo periodo (1.6%). En su interior destacó el alza de 12.2% anual para maquinaria y equipo, también superior a su crecimiento histórico promedio de 5.0%.
* En 2022, la población ocupada creció en 2.4 millones respecto a 2021 y la tasa de desempleo promedio del año fue de las más bajas desde que se tiene registro, al ubicarse en 3.3%.
* En el mismo año, se registraron 753 mil nuevas plazas ante el IMSS, principalmente de carácter permanente. Esta cifra es la tercera más alta desde 1997. La población trabajadora se benefició de un incremento al salario promedio real de 2.7% anual.
* En lo que va del sexenio (dic. de 2018 a dic. de 2022), se han creado 1.3 millones de empleos ante el IMSS, de los cuales la mayoría corresponde a empleo permanente. Esta cifra es superior a las registradas en los sexenios de Felipe Calderón y Vicente Fox para el mismo periodo de tiempo.
* El comercio exterior de México en 2022 alcanzó un máximo histórico de 1.2 billones de dólares, en particular por los niveles máximos de exportaciones manufactureras, así como de las importaciones de bienes intermedios y de capital. Dentro de la IED, las nuevas inversiones registraron el segundo mayor monto después de 2013, de 14 mil millones de dólares.
* Tanto mexicanos como extranjeros están regresando a invertir en el país. Con cifras al tercer trimestre de 2022, se observó un mayor apetito para invertir en México con lo cual se observó una menor salida de capitales por 19 mil millones de dólares respecto a 2021.

* En 2022, el Gobierno Federal obtuvo ingresos adicionales al programa en 632 mil millones de pesos, de los cuales 397 mil millones de pesos correspondieron a la menor recaudación por el estímulo al IEPS de combustibles.

# Evidence Paper — AMLO, Mexico, 2022, Chapter 5B

**Source:** "Comunicado No. 9 — Informes sobre la Situación Económica, las Finanzas Públicas y la Deuda Pública al cuarto trimestre de 2022," Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público (SHCP), published 30 January 2023. Government executive press release (Comunicado) on the gob.mx portal. URL: https://www.gob.mx/shcp/prensa/comunicado-no-9-informes-sobre-la-situacion-economica-las-finanzas-publicas-y-la-deuda-publica-al-cuarto-trimestre-de-2022

**Source role:** executive_official_report (self-report of the Treasury on the macro-fiscal outcome of the fourth year of the AMLO administration).

**Important caveats on source perspective:** This is a SHCP-issued press release. It is what the executive branch chose to publish about its own fiscal year. Every quantitative claim below is the Executive's own presentation; the document does not include independent methodological notes, dissenting internal commentary, or comparisons with audit/court findings. It is also a quarterly summary, not a technical annex: claims about distributional incidence, regulatory enforcement, or quality of public services are not themselves present in this document. The paper documents what the source asserts; the reader must weigh that against the absence of contrary material in this single artifact.

---

## 5B.1 — Legislative agenda, formal policies, and executed budgets: broad-based sustainable prosperity vs. rents, loyalty purchases, or short-term popularity

The source itself does not describe AMLO's legislative agenda. It describes the **executed fiscal outcome** of 2022, which the SHCP frames as "un manejo responsable de los recursos públicos, un nivel estable de la deuda y un ejercicio eficiente del gasto orientado al bienestar de las familias mexicanas" (introductory paragraph, lead of press release).

Concrete fiscal composition the report itself provides for 2022:
- Total public spending: 7 trillion 569 billion pesos, +4.1% real y/y, equal to 26.5% of GDP (executive-summary block). This is described as "tres años de crecimientos consecutivos" of public spending.
- Social protection spending: +8.7% real y/y, 5.3% of GDP — described as "un nuevo máximo histórico" (executive-summary block).
- Physical investment (inversión física): +25.2% real annual growth — described as "el crecimiento más alto desde el 2009"; reached 3.3% of GDP, "su nivel más alto desde 2016" (executive-summary block).
- Revenue: 6.595 trillion pesos, 422 billion pesos above the program; +2.5% versus 2021 (tax-revenue block).
- Tax policy posture: "sin aumentar o crear impuestos nuevos" (executive-summary block).
- IEPS fuel subsidy: government absorbed 397 billion pesos less in IEPS-fuel revenue than programmed (tax-revenue block).

The source claims the 2022 fiscal stance combined (a) tax stability / no new taxes, (b) high social-protection growth, (c) the strongest physical-investment growth since 2009, and (d) a primary balance at –0.5% of GDP and a public deficit of –3.4% of GDP (fiscal-aggregates block).

**What the source does not contain:** No legislative-bill tally, no enumeration of social programs (e.g., Programas para el Bienestar), no program-level incidence analysis, no comparison of infrastructure portfolio composition between productive and patronage projects. The "bienestar de las familias mexicanas" framing is a stated objective, not a measured outcome in this document.

---

## 5B.2 — Appointment of qualified economic professionals, operational independence, retention vs. loyalty

The source does not address personnel decisions at all. There is no mention of Health Ministry / Banco de México / SAT / CNBV / CFE / Pemex appointments, qualifications, tenure, removal, or independence. No names of economic officials appear beyond the institutional attribution to SHCP itself.

This is a structural absence of the document — it is a quarterly macroeconomic communiqué, not a governance personnel report. Any inference about 5B.2 from this single artifact would be unsupported.

---

## 5B.3 — Fiscal, tax, debt, monetary, and financial rules: enacted, administered, complied with; protection of macro stability and long-term investment

The document is centrally a fiscal-rules compliance report for 2022. Concrete anchors:

- Public debt (deuda pública): 49.4% of GDP at end-2022. The SHCP emphasizes this is **1.6 pp below the 2022 budget target** and **1.4 pp below 2021**. The report attributes the gap to "buen desempeño de los ingresos presupuestarios, que aún después del subsidio al IEPS, fueron mayores a lo presupuestado en 1.5% del PIB" (introductory paragraph).
- Fiscal aggregates (% of GDP, 2022):
  - Primary balance: –0.5%
  - Public deficit (déficit público): –3.4%
  - Public-Sector Financial Requirements (RFSP): 4.4%
  (Executive-summary block.)
- Fiscal buffers ("blindaje de amortiguadores fiscales"): jointly **USD 262 billion**, composed of international reserves, the IMF Flexible Credit Line (Línea de Crédito Flexible), the Federal Reserve swap line (Línea "Swap" with the Fed), and stabilization funds. The SHCP presents this as a shock-absorption shield (executive-summary block).
- Debt-management operations in 2022 (debt-market block):
  - 7 October 2022: buyback auction of 68,017 million pesos of debt maturing 2023–2046, paired with a sale auction of 48,596 million pesos of long-term Bonos and Udibonos.
  - 30 November 2022: third placement of Bondes G — 7,090 million pesos at 1-year, 2,660 million pesos at 2-year, 250 million pesos at 3-year.
  - 7 December 2022: new Bono M maturing May 2033, 12,500 million pesos, 7.5% coupon.
  - 8 December 2022: Bono M placement with 2033 and 2053 maturities, 50,863 million pesos, plus a buyback of Bonos M with 2029–2047 maturities.
- Debt-profile result: "Para 2023, y los subsecuentes dos años, las presiones de deuda se redujeron en promedio 73%, debido a distintas operaciones de recompra. De esta manera se liberaron recursos por 3 mil millones de dólares para la siguiente administración" (debt-market block). This is a forward-looking maturity-profile claim made by SHCP.
- Sovereign-rating posture: "México … mantiene el grado de inversión y una perspectiva estable de parte de las 8 calificadoras que evalúan la deuda" (debt-market block). Mexico is said to have received 21 international awards for debt-management strategy over the four years of the administration.
- Tax-rule posture described: "El combate a la evasión fiscal continúa reflejándose positivamente en los ingresos tributarios, sin aumentar o crear impuestos nuevos" (tax-revenue block).
- No discussion of monetary policy (Banxico independence), financial-regulation rules (CNBV), or debt-rule legislation itself (e.g., Ley de Disciplina Financiera de las Entidades Federativas y Municipios or the Federal Budget and Fiscal Responsibility Law) is included in the press release.

The SHCP self-frames the 2022 outcome as compliant with the fiscal trajectory: lower-than-budgeted debt-to-GDP, deficit levels stated as percentages of GDP, and an explicit buffer inventory. The 2022 deficit (3.4% of GDP) is presented as a fact, not adjudicated against any specific numeric rule.

---

## 5B.4 — Fair, enforceable rules for competition, entrepreneurship, property, trade, investment, job creation

The source does not enumerate laws or regulations in these areas. It does report **outcomes** that the SHCP attributes to the investment climate:

- Private consumption: +7.1% y/y through October 2022, more than double its historical average (2.7%); services consumption at pre-pandemic levels (macroeconomic block).
- Gross fixed investment (inversión fija bruta): +5.5% y/y through October — "superior al promedio histórico para un mismo periodo (1.6%)". Within that, machinery and equipment: +12.2% y/y, vs. 5.0% historical average (macroeconomic block).
- Job creation: 753,000 new IMSS-registered positions in 2022 — "la tercera más alta desde 1997"; mostly permanent. The sexenio (Dec 2018–Dec 2022) total is 1.3 million IMSS jobs, which the source says exceeds the equivalent four-year totals of the Calderón and Fox administrations (labor-market block).
- Real average wage: +2.7% real annual (labor-market block).
- Foreign Direct Investment: USD 32 billion through Q3 2022 — "nivel no visto desde 2013". Within FDI, "nuevas inversiones" reached USD 14 billion, the second-highest figure after 2013 (trade/FDI block).
- Capital flight: net outflow was USD 19 billion lower than in 2021, which the SHCP attributes to greater appetite for investing in Mexico (trade/FDI block).
- Foreign trade: USD 1.2 trillion in 2022 — "máximo histórico" — driven by record manufacturing exports and record imports of intermediate and capital goods (trade/FDI block).

The SHCP presents these as evidence of an attractive investment and trade environment. The document does not describe any specific regulatory reform (e.g., new competition law, new investment law, new labor-reform enforcement record) that produced these outcomes. The 753,000 IMSS jobs figure and the +2.7% real wage are the only labor-market-rule outputs the source identifies.

---

## 5B.5 — Competition, procurement, disclosure, anti-corruption enforcement against politically connected actors; cooperation with audits and courts; remedy of proven favoritism

The source does not address anti-corruption enforcement, procurement rules, ASF (Auditoría Superior de la Federación) results, court cooperation, or any politically-connected-firm case. The only adjacent material is the indirect fiscal statement:

- "El combate a la evasión fiscal continúa reflejándose positivamente en los ingresos tributarios, sin aumentar o crear impuestos nuevos" (tax-revenue block).
- Tax revenues excluding the IEPS-fuel line: 13.6% of GDP — "el mayor nivel desde que se tiene registro"; +7.8% real y/y ("la mayor tasa desde 2016") (tax-revenue block).
- ISR: 2.270 trillion pesos (8.0% of GDP), historical record; +11% real y/y, the largest growth since 2016 (tax-revenue block).
- IVA: 1.222 trillion pesos, 4.3% of GDP, above the 3.9% historical average (tax-revenue block).

These numbers describe the **revenue effect** of tax administration and evasion enforcement; they do not describe any anti-corruption case, sanction, debarment, or audit finding. The document is silent on 5B.5's specific subjects.

---

## 5B.6 — Budget execution: timely, high-quality infrastructure, education, health, technology, administrative capacity, predictable regulation

The source provides spending aggregates but not program-level execution quality or timeliness:

- Public spending growth: +4.1% real y/y in 2022; 26.5% of GDP (executive-summary block).
- Social protection: +8.7% real y/y; 5.3% of GDP — described as a historic high (executive-summary block).
- Physical investment (inversión física): +25.2% real annual growth — "el crecimiento más alto desde el 2009"; 3.3% of GDP, highest since 2016 (executive-summary block).
- Participaciones to states and municipalities: largest amount on record; +7.3% real y/y (executive-summary block).
- Procurement data, completion timelines, project-level disbursement schedules, or quality indicators for education/health/road/tech projects are not in the source.

The SHCP frames the 2022 fiscal stance as both "orientado al bienestar" (welfare-oriented) and as the highest physical-investment growth in 13 years. The document does not break the "inversión física" figure into education, health, transport, energy, or technology components — it is a single aggregate.

---

## 5B.7 — Reliable economic information, independent evaluation and audit, correction of failed programs

The source positions itself as a release of quarterly fiscal information by SHCP. The body of the release is the information itself. Indicators of transparency posture in the document:

- Reference for further detail: "Para obtener información más detallada, se pueden consultar las estadísticas de finanzas y deuda pública en el sitio de internet: http://presto.hacienda.gob.mx/EstoporLayout/estadisticas.jsp" (closing paragraph).
- Sovereign-rating transparency framing: "México … mantiene el grado de inversión y una perspectiva estable de parte de las 8 calificadoras que evalúan la deuda" (debt-market block) — implying external evaluation by all eight rating agencies that cover Mexico.
- Award tally: "21 reconocimientos internacionales por la estrategia del manejo de deuda" over the four years (debt-market block).

The document does not describe:
- Publication of internal audit findings (ASF),
- A response to a specific audit or independent evaluation,
- Correction of any program following evidence of failure,
- Any retraction, methodology change, or post-publication correction.

The release itself is a single instance of the administration publishing its own quarterly outcome; the source does not present evidence of how the administration **responds** to evaluations that contradict it.

---

## 5B.8 — Distribution of gains and burdens across classes, regions, genders, groups

The source supplies a small number of distributional data points, framed at the aggregate level:

- Real wage: +2.7% real annual (labor-market block). This is the average wage at IMSS-registered jobs; the source does not provide wage deciles.
- Unemployment rate: 2.8% total, 2.5% for women — "las tasas de desempleo más bajas en 17 años" (labor-market block). The female-specific figure is one of the few gender-distinguished data points in the release.
- 2.4 million jobs created in 2022, "en su mayoría formales" (labor-market block). Formal/informal split is not broken out further.
- Sexenio total: 1.3 million IMSS jobs, compared with Calderón and Fox equivalents (labor-market block). Regional breakdown is not provided.
- Social protection spending: 5.3% of GDP, a historic high (executive-summary block). No program-by-program breakdown (e.g., pensions, anti-poverty transfers, child support) is in the source.
- Federal transfers to states/municipalities (participaciones): real +7.3% y/y, historic high (executive-summary block). No state-level incidence.
- Tax incidence: ISR growth (+11% real) is attributed in part to "el incremento en los salarios reales" (tax-revenue block). No progressivity, regressivity, or sectoral analysis is provided.

The release is largely national-aggregate. Class-, region-, and gender-distributional claims are limited to the unemployment-by-gender split and the "bienestar" framing of social-protection spending.

---

## 5B.9 — Response to shocks: timely, funded, transparently targeted measures; monitoring and correction

The source names the 2022 shock environment and the Executive's response posture:

- External shock context identified by SHCP: "disrupciones en las cadenas de suministro y los costos de transporte" decreased in 2022, "lo cual aminoró las presiones inflacionarias" (executive-summary block). This is the SHCP's own framing of the inflation episode; the document does not present inflation rate figures, real-wage erosion numbers, or poverty incidence.
- Global slowdown risk: SHCP projects 2023 global growth of 2.1% y/y, expected to be supported by China's reopening and lower commodity prices (executive-summary block).
- Hedge against future shocks: "Nuestro país cuenta con un blindaje de amortiguadores fiscales para hacer frente a los choques económicos tanto internos como externos, el cual asciende de manera conjunta a 262 mil millones de dólares. Al interior destacan las reservas internacionales, la Línea de Crédito Flexible con el FMI, la Línea 'Swap' con la Reserva Federal de los EE.UU. y los fondos de estabilización" (executive-summary block). These are pre-arranged buffers, not new allocations.
- Counter-cyclical oil-price shock absorber: oil revenues were 1.482 trillion pesos (5.2% of GDP) — "el nivel más alto observado desde 2014"; +18.7% real y/y (tax-revenue block). The high oil-price year is presented as a fiscal windfall.
- Counter-cyclical energy-price shock absorber: IEPS-fuel subsidy absorbed 397 billion pesos of foregone revenue vs. the program (tax-revenue block). This is the price-control / consumer-subsidy response to high fuel prices; the source frames it as "menor recaudación por el estímulo al IEPS de combustibles," not as a quantified transfer to households.
- Debt-maturity response: 7 October and 8 December 2022 buybacks in 2023–2046 and 2029–2047 paper. The 73% reduction in 2023-2025 debt pressure is a pre-emptive liability-management action (debt-market block).
- USD 3 billion released for the next administration via 2022 buybacks (debt-market block).
- No specific monitoring indicators, ex-post evaluation of a 2022 measure, or correction of a measure in 2022 are described in the release.

The document is a forward-declaration of buffers and a backward-declaration of completed actions; it does not present mid-year course corrections or formal monitoring outputs.

---

## 5B.10 — Stronger and more durable economic trajectory than inherited

The source supports an "improvement" narrative with the following comparisons:

- 2022 GDP growth: 2.9% through November — "mejor desempeño que el esperado por los analistas" (introductory paragraph). The source does not state the inherited (2018) growth rate for comparison; it notes the 2022 print beat expectations.
- 2022 unemployment: 2.8% total, 2.5% for women; 3.3% annual average — "de las más bajas desde que se tiene registro" (labor-market block).
- 2022 IMSS-formal job creation: 753,000 — third-highest since 1997 (labor-market block).
- Sexenio (Dec 2018–Dec 2022) IMSS job creation: 1.3 million — "superior a las registradas en los sexenios de Felipe Calderón y Vicente Fox para el mismo periodo de tiempo" (labor-market block). This is the only directly inherited-to-current comparison in the release.
- 2022 trade: USD 1.2 trillion — historical record (trade/FDI block).
- FDI through Q3 2022: USD 32 billion — highest since 2013 (introducción).
- 2022 oil revenues: 5.2% of GDP — highest since 2014 (tax-revenue block).
- 2022 tax revenue ex-IEPS-fuel: 13.6% of GDP — "el mayor nivel desde que se tiene registro" (tax-revenue block).
- 2022 ISR: 2.270 trillion pesos (8.0% of GDP) — historical record (tax-revenue block).
- IVA: 4.3% of GDP — above 3.9% historical average (tax-revenue block).
- 2022 physical investment: 3.3% of GDP — highest since 2016 (executive-summary block).
- 2022 social protection: 5.3% of GDP — historic high (executive-summary block).
- End-2022 public debt: 49.4% of GDP — 1.4 pp lower than 2021 (introducción).
- Forward debt-pressure metric: 73% reduction in 2023–2025 debt pressures (debt-market block).
- Sovereign-rating posture: investment grade maintained with stable outlook from all eight rating agencies (debt-market block).

**Trajectory framing language used by the source:** "Al cierre del cuarto año de la administración, las finanzas públicas continúan con un manejo responsable de los recursos públicos, un nivel estable de la deuda y un ejercicio eficiente del gasto orientado al bienestar de las familias mexicanas" (introducción). The grammar ("continúan") presents 2022 as continuation of an existing four-year pattern, not a new departure.

**What the source does not contain for 5B.10:**
- A 2018 baseline numerical comparison for most aggregates (debt, productivity, exports, FDI, formal employment).
- Total Factor Productivity trend.
- Investment-to-GDP series for the sexenio.
- Distributional/Gini comparison.
- Implementation-lag analysis for any infrastructure project.
- External-conditions decomposition (oil price, US monetary policy, nearshoring cycle) — although oil prices are referenced as a revenue driver, the report does not break out how much of 2022's result is oil-attributable vs. non-oil.
- Independent assessment of fiscal sustainability beyond the SHCP's own RFSP/balance aggregates.

The comparative claim the source itself makes explicitly is the sexenio IMSS-job creation versus Calderón and Fox (labor-market block). All other "historical high / highest since X" claims are point-in-time statements, not inherited-to-current trajectories.

---

## Source-level notes for the judge

- **Type of document:** Quarterly macroeconomic press release (Comunicado No. 9). It is the executive summary, not the underlying technical report.
- **Author:** Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, the Treasury of the federal government. Self-reporting.
- **Date:** 30 January 2023; data cover Q4 2022 / full-year 2022 (with some indicators through October or November 2022).
- **What the source is best at:** Forward-looking fiscal aggregates (debt, deficit, RFSP, buffers), revenue composition, debt-market operations with dates and amounts, and selected labor-market and trade outcomes.
- **What the source does not address:** Legislative agenda specifics, personnel appointments, regulatory enforcement, anti-corruption actions, audit findings, program-level execution quality, distributional incidence beyond gender unemployment, independent evaluation, and any inherited-baseline quantitative comparison except the IMSS job-creation series vs. Calderón and Fox.
- **Locator phrasing:** Bullets in the paper are tagged to the press-release section (e.g., "tax-revenue block," "debt-market block," "labor-market block," "macroeconomic block," "executive-summary block," "introducción," "closing paragraph") rather than to the original HTML unit numbers, because the source is a single short document with one canonical paragraphs ordering. The original document is reproduced verbatim above and may be re-read by the judge.
- **Target period:** The release is the 2022 year-end fiscal outcome (Q4 2022). Many indicators are stated as full-year 2022, some as through October 2022, some as through Q3 2022. The judge should treat year-2022 anchors as the default and use the indicator-specific dates when finer resolution is needed.
